headings.title: Introduction to Skilled Nursing Facilities
headings.content: A **Skilled Nursing Facility (SNF)** provides round-the-clock medical care and rehabilitation for individuals who require a higher level of assistance than can be safely managed at home or in a basic assisted living environment. Unlike standard residential care homes, an SNF is staffed continuously by licensed healthcare professionals, including registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, and physical therapists. Patients typically arrive following a hospital stay for acute conditions, surgeries, or severe exacerbations of chronic illnesses, staying either for short-term restorative rehabilitation or long-term custodial care.

headings.title: Services and Levels of Care Provided
headings.content:
Care within an SNF spans a broad spectrum, ranging from short-term rehabilitative therapies to complex chronic disease management. Services are categorized into specific clinical domains:

- **Skilled Nursing**: Wound care management, intravenous therapy, catheter maintenance, and complex medication administration.
- **Rehabilitation Therapies**: Physical therapy for mobility, occupational therapy for daily living skills, and speech-language pathology for swallowing and communication disorders.
- **Custodial Support**: Assistance with activities of daily living such as bathing, dressing, and feeding for residents with permanent functional deficits.
- **Palliative Care**: Comfort-focused symptom management for individuals with terminal or advanced progressive illnesses.

headings.title: Admission Criteria and Patient Eligibility
headings.content: Admission to a skilled nursing facility is governed by strict clinical and financial guidelines. Generally, a patient must have experienced a qualifying hospital stay of at least three consecutive days for an acute condition before entering the facility for Medicare-covered short-term rehabilitation. The physician must formally certify that the patient requires daily skilled nursing or therapy services. Preadmission screenings evaluate the resident's medical stability, cognitive status, and behavioral health needs to ensure the facility possesses the adequate resources and staffing competencies to deliver safe, effective care.

headings.title: The Role of the Nursing Team in SNFs
headings.content: The nursing staff forms the backbone of daily operations in a skilled nursing facility. Registered Nurses assume leadership responsibilities, overseeing care delivery, managing clinical emergencies, and supervising licensed practical nurses and nursing assistants. Licensed Practical Nurses administer medications, monitor vital signs, and perform routine treatments. Certified Nursing Assistants provide the vital hands-on support for personal hygiene, mobility, and nutritional intake. Because nurses spend the most time with residents, they act as the primary observers of subtle clinical changes, noting early signs of decline such as confusion, skin breakdown, or subtle respiratory distress.

headings.title: Interdisciplinary Healthcare Collaboration
headings.content: Comprehensive resident care requires seamless coordination among diverse professional disciplines. The interdisciplinary team typically includes the attending physician, charge nurse, physical and occupational therapists, speech-language pathologists, registered dietitians, social workers, and the activities director. Regular care conferences bring these professionals together with the resident and their family to review progress, adjust goals, and address emerging challenges. Effective communication prevents fragmented care, reduces medication errors, and ensures that physical, emotional, and social needs are addressed holistically.

headings.title: Patient Assessment, Care Planning, and Documentation
headings.content: Clinical documentation in skilled nursing facilities is highly structured and federally regulated. Upon admission, nurses complete comprehensive baseline assessments covering skin integrity, fall risk, nutritional status, and cognitive function. These findings feed into standardized assessment instruments, such as the Minimum Data Set, which guides the creation of the individualized care plan. Accurate, timely charting is legally mandatory to track treatment efficacy, justify continued insurance reimbursement, and communicate clinical shifts across shift changes.

headings.title: Rehabilitation and Restorative Nursing Care
headings.content: Restorative nursing bridges the gap between formal therapy sessions and everyday independence. While physical and occupational therapists design specialized recovery regimens, nursing personnel reinforce these techniques during routine daily activities. For example, nurses encourage residents to use adaptive feeding equipment during meals or practice safe transfer mechanics when getting out of bed. The goal is to prevent functional decline, maintain existing physical capacities, and promote maximum autonomy, thereby preventing the complications associated with immobility such as contractures and pressure ulcers.

headings.title: Regulations, Quality Standards, and Safety
headings.content: Skilled nursing facilities operate under rigorous federal and state oversight to protect resident rights and safety. Regulatory bodies inspect facilities regularly for compliance with health codes, infection control protocols, and medication management standards. Facilities must maintain safe staffing ratios, secure environmental controls, and robust emergency preparedness plans for events such as power outages or natural disasters. Incident reporting systems track falls, medication errors, and grievances, driving continuous quality improvement initiatives across the organization.

headings.title: Transition of Care and Discharge Planning
headings.content: Discharge planning begins on the day of admission, ensuring a seamless transition from the skilled nursing facility to the next care setting, whether that is private home living, assisted living, or specialized hospice care. The interdisciplinary team evaluates the resident's home environment, arranges necessary durable medical equipment like hospital beds or walkers, coordinates outpatient therapy referrals, and educates family caregivers on medication management. Thorough discharge education significantly reduces preventable hospital readmissions and empowers residents to maintain their highest possible level of independence.
